growth_story.headline: Eritrea's early gains after independence were undone by war with Ethiopia and a long standoff; by 2011 income per person was about where it was in 1994.
growth_story.arc: After independence, income per person grew fast, and from 1993 to 2001 it rose 3.9 percent a year on average. It peaked in 1998, the year a border war with Ethiopia began; the IMF says the war drastically changed the economy's path, cutting off Ethiopia as an export market and driving up public debt. From 2002 to 2011 growth averaged -1.6 percent a year, as the country stayed mobilized in a "no war, no peace" standoff, with labour shortages, less trade and more state control. A severe drought made 2008 the worst year in the record, at -12.1 percent, before growth picked up to 6.7 percent in 2011, the last year in the data. By then income per person was still 16.4 percent below the 1998 peak, about where it first was in 1994. The World Bank now describes an economy that relies on mining exports, where state-owned firms dominate, emerging from long isolation after UN sanctions were lifted in 2018.

threads.title: Border war with Ethiopia
threads.text: The 1998 to 2000 war with Ethiopia ended a promising start after independence. Output fell, public debt rose fast, and Eritrea lost Ethiopia, its traditional export market.

citations.title: Fiscal Sustainability: The Case of Eritrea (IMF Working Paper WP/04/7)
citations.quote: Following a promising start after independence in 1993, the war with Ethiopia during 1998-2000 drastically changed the performance of the Eritrean economy: GDP declined,

citations.title: Fiscal Sustainability: The Case of Eritrea (IMF Working Paper WP/04/7)
citations.quote: Since 1998, current account deficits have widened mainly as a result of the loss of the traditional export market of Ethiopia

threads.title: No war, no peace
threads.text: After the war the border conflict stayed unresolved and the country stayed mobilized. Labour shortages and reduced trade weighed on the economy, and the state stepped up its control, including price controls. A severe drought in 2008 cut the harvest sharply.

citations.title: Eritrea Health and Education Sectors: Public Expenditure Review 2008
citations.quote: In this climate of instability, with labor shortages (as a result of mobilization) and reduced trade, the economy has been under strain.

citations.title: Eritrea Health and Education Sectors: Public Expenditure Review 2008
citations.quote: The government has responded through increased state intervention in the economy and the introduction of price controls.

citations.title: Public Information Notice: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2009 Article IV Consultation with the State of Eritrea
citations.quote: Severe drought in 2008 resulted in a harvest that was "one-fourth of that of the previous year"

threads.title: Isolation and the state's reach
threads.text: UN sanctions left Eritrea in long isolation until 2018, and growth leaned on domestic sources. The World Bank says state-owned firms and regulation still hold back private investment.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Eritrea, October 2026
citations.quote: Following the lifting of the United Nations (UN) sanctions in 2018, Eritrea emerged from prolonged isolation, having relied largely on domestic growth.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Eritrea, October 2026
citations.quote: Private sector investment remains constrained by state-owned enterprise dominance and regulatory restrictions.

threads.title: Mining and the Colluli mine
threads.text: Zinc, copper and gold now earn almost all of Eritrea's export income, so metal prices swing the economy. A Chinese firm bought half of the Colluli potash mine in 2023, and the World Bank expects it to start producing by end-2027.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Eritrea, October 2026
citations.quote: These three minerals account for more than 95 percent of Eritrea’s export earnings.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Eritrea, October 2026
citations.quote: Exports are highly concentrated in zinc, copper, and gold, exposing the economy to commodity price swings and changes in demand from China.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Eritrea, October 2026
citations.quote: In early 2023, the Chinese company Sichuan Road and Bridge Group acquired a 50 percent stake in the Colluli potash mine

threads.title: A heavy public debt
threads.text: The war years drove up public debt, both at home and abroad. The World Bank says most of it is now owed to domestic banks and describes the country as in debt distress.

citations.title: Fiscal Sustainability: The Case of Eritrea (IMF Working Paper WP/04/7)
citations.quote: However, the most significant change was the sharp deterioration of the public finances and rapid increase in domestic and external public debt,

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook for Eritrea: April 2024
citations.quote: Public debt was estimated at around 219 percent of GDP at end-2023, of which nearly 80 percent is owed to domestic banks.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook for Eritrea: April 2024
citations.quote: The country is in debt distress

since_last_year.text: The World Bank reports that strong mining output and household spending lifted growth in 2025. It also notes work begun in September 2025 to upgrade the two main power stations, and lists recent tensions with Ethiopia among the risks.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Eritrea, October 2026
citations.quote: Real GDP growth increased to 3.2 percent in 2025, supported by strong mining output and private consumption

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Eritrea, October 2026
citations.quote: In September 2025, Eritrea embarked on upgrading of its two main power stations at Beleza and Hirgigo

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes modest, mining-supported growth in recent years, but the data here end in 2011, and the World Bank itself says national accounts are unpublished. So the record cannot show whether recent growth has lifted income per person above its 1998 peak. The World Bank also expects income per person to grow only slowly.
